title: StepPO: Step-Aligned Policy Optimization for Agentic Reinforcement Learning

paper.title: StepPO: Step-Aligned Policy Optimization for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
paper.abstract: Abstract General agents have given rise to phenomenal applications such as OpenClaw and Claude Code. As these agent systems (a.k.a. Harnesses) strive for bolder goals, they demand increasingly stronger agentic capabilities from foundation Large Language Models (LLMs). Agentic Reinforcement Learning (RL) is emerging as a central post-training paradigm for empowering LLMs with these capabilities and is playing an increasingly pivotal role in agent training. Unlike single-turn token-level alignment or reasoning enhancement, as in RLHF and RLVR, Agentic RL targets multi-turn interactive settings, where the goal is to optimize core agentic capabilities such as decision making and tool use while addressing new challenges including delayed and sparse rewards, as well as long and variable context. As a result, the token-centric modeling and optimization paradigm inherited from traditional LLM RL is becoming increasingly inadequate for capturing real LLM agent behavior. In this paper, we present StepPO as a position on step-level Agentic RL. We argue that the conventional token-level Markov Decision Process (MDP) should be advanced to a step-level MDP formulation, and that the step, rather than the token, should be regarded as the proper action representation for LLM agents. We then propose step-level credit assignment as the natural optimization counterpart of this formulation, thereby aligning policy optimization and reward propagation with the granularity of agent decisions. Finally, we discuss the key systems designs required to realize step-level Agentic RL in practice and preliminary experiments provide initial evidence for the effectiveness of this perspective. We hope that the step-aligned, step-level paradigm embodied in StepPO offers the Agentic RL community a useful lens for understanding agent behavior and helps advance LLMs toward stronger general-agent capabilities.

Table 1 : Representative methods differ in how they place the MDP formulation and credit-assignment units, revealing a granularity mismatch in Agentic RL. StepPO reduces this mismatch by aligning both with the interaction step. Method MDP formulation granularity Credit assignment granularity PPO [ 20 ] Token-level Token-level Reinforce++ [ 11 ] Token-level Token-level GRPO [ 26 ] Token-level Trajectory-level RLOO [ 4 ] Token-level Trajectory-level LightningRL [ 17 ] Step-level Trajectory-level StepPO Step-level Step-level 1 Introduction General agents built on Large Language Models (LLMs) [ 1 , 6 ] have already given rise to phenomenal applications [ 8 ] such as OpenClaw and Claude Code [ 19 , 5 ] . As these agent systems strive for bolder goals, they place increasing demands on the underlying models to support agentic capabilities such as decision making, planning, tool use [ 37 , 23 ] , environment interaction [ 36 , 29 ] , and long-horizon task execution [ 8 , 38 , 16 , 31 ] . Once optimization targets this regime, the problem is no longer only how to score a final answer, but also how to model the decision process that produces sustained behavior across many interaction rounds. This is why Agentic Reinforcement Learning (RL) is becoming a central post-training paradigm for LLM agents [ 34 , 7 , 38 ] . Earlier recipes such as Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) [ 20 ] and Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) [ 26 ] were largely developed around single responses or short reasoning traces. By contrast, Agentic RL targets multi-turn interaction with tools and environments, where the training objective must directly shape decision making, action selection, and adaptation under feedback. In this setting, delayed and sparse rewards, long-horizon interaction, and long, variable context all become first-class challenges, and the token-centric paradigm inherited from conventional LLM RL becomes increasingly inadequate for capturing real agent behavior. In this paper, we present StepPO , as a perspective on Agentic RL built around step-level agent behavior. Our central claim begins with the formal abstraction of the decision process. The conventional token-level Markov Decision Process (MDP) formulation remains natural for autoregressive language modeling [ 20 ] , but individual tokens are too fine-grained to serve as the right abstraction for multi-turn decision making, tool coordination, and environment-mediated state transitions. We therefore argue that Agentic RL should move from token-level MDP to step-level MDP, where each complete interaction round, rather than each token, forms the proper transition unit and the step becomes the right action representation for LLM agents. This shift in MDP formulation also requires a corresponding shift in trajectory representation and optimization. Multi-turn agents have often been recorded as growing messages and later reconstructed as text for training [ 14 ] . That representation is convenient, but it hides a serious inconsistency: rollout happens in token space [ 15 , 25 ] , whereas training may depend on a second tokenization pass over reconstructed text [ 39 , 28 ] . Because the mapping from tokens to text and back to tokens is not reversible in general, such pipelines can suffer from retokenization drift, breaking rollout-training consistency and destabilizing step-aligned learning [ 7 , 13 ] . Once the interaction step becomes the basic unit of behavior, the natural optimization counterpart should also align with that unit. In conventional Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) [ 24 ] , credit is typically propagated at token granularity, whereas in Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) style training [ 26 , 40 ] , the signal is more naturally attached at trajectory granularity. Token-level credit is often too local and noisy, while trajectory-level credit is often too coarse to identify the contribution of intermediate decisions [ 32 , 21 ] . StepPO emphasizes step-aligned policy optimization through step-level credit assignment, aligning reward propagation with the same interaction unit used for decision making. The same transition extends beyond modeling and optimization to the training system itself. Step-level Agentic RL must support heterogeneous agents, preserve step-native data, manage trajectories and rewards across a centralized data layer, reduce redundant computation in long contexts, and coordinate asynchronous generation and training [ 10 , 17 ] . This systems perspective also motivates our research path from Agent-R1 to Claw-R1, where the former foregrounds training abstraction and token-space consistency [ 7 , 2 ] , while the latter foregrounds gateway-centered data management and heterogeneous-agent support [ 3 , 18 ] . To complement this position with concrete evidence, we provide HotpotQA [ 35 ] experiments showing that StepPO consistently outperforms token-level PPO in a multi-step agent setting. Table 1 summarizes the perspective advanced in this paper. Our position is that Agentic RL is undergoing a coordinated shift from token-level to step-level formulation across MDP design, trajectory representation, credit assignment, and systems support, and that StepPO offers a step-aligned optimization lens for this shift. The rest of the paper develops this view in order: Section 2 situates StepPO in prior work, Section 3 argues for step-level MDP, Section 4 revisits trajectory representation, Section 5 discusses step-level credit assignment, Section 6 turns to training systems, Section 7 traces the path from Agent-R1 to Claw-R1, Section 8 presents preliminary empirical evidence, and Section 9 concludes with broader implications for step-level Agentic RL. 2 Related Work This section situates StepPO in the broader evolution of the field. We first review reinforcement learning for LLMs, then trace how Agentic RL algorithms and training frameworks gradually moved from token-level generation toward interaction-aware optimization and systems design. This progression helps clarify both what StepPO inherits from prior work and where it departs from earlier formulations. 2.1 Reinforcement Learning for Large Language Model Modern reinforcement learning for LLMs begins with single-turn post-training recipes such as RLHF [ 20 ] , PPO [ 24 ] , and RLVR or group-based variants such as GRPO [ 26 ] . In these settings, token-level optimization is a natural abstraction because the policy is trained to produce one response conditioned on one prompt, with little or no intermediate environment structure. What these approaches share is not a single optimizer but a common assumption: the semantically meaningful action remains closely aligned with token generation. That assumption becomes increasingly strained once the target changes from single-turn response generation to long-horizon agent interaction. In multi-turn settings, the policy no longer merely continues a sequence; it completes one interaction round, triggers environment changes, and conditions on new observations. This shift is what makes step-level Agentic RL a distinct problem rather than a straightforward extension of conventional LLM post-training. 2.2 Agentic RL Algorithms The algorithmic evolution of Agentic RL has moved progressively from adapting RL to agent settings toward redefining the interaction unit itself. Early forward-looking work such as Search-R1 [ 14 ] and RAGEN [ 34 ] already exposed the difficulty of training multi-turn agents under sparse reward, long horizons, and environment feedback. More recent methods made this shift explicit in the optimizer: Tree Search for LLM Agent Reinforcement Learning proposes Tree-GRPO, which combines tree search with grouped relative policy optimization so that branching agent trajectories can receive more informative training signals [ 12 ] ; PaperScout defines Proximal Sequence Policy Optimization over complete interaction responses rather than isolated tokens [ 21 ] ; GiGPO introduces a finer-grained group-based mechanism for agent credit assignment [ 9 ] ; Agent Lightning formulates arbitrary agent execution traces as MDP transitions and emphasizes transition-level decomposition [ 17 ] ; and the broader ecosystem represented by Let It Flow likewise shifts attention from raw token streams to semantically meaningful interaction chunks [ 33 ] . Taken together, these works show a clear industry trend: once the optimization target becomes real agent behavior, the learning problem must be organized around interaction-aware decisions rather than token-level continuation alone. 2.3 Agentic RL Training Frameworks In parallel with algorithmic work, Agentic RL training frameworks have become a research topic in their own right. A useful starting point is veRL, whose underlying HybridFlow system frames RLHF as a flexible dataflow problem and provides an efficient general-purpose RL foundation for LLM post-training [ 27 ] .
